inserts.title: Direction is judged from the moth's path
paragraphs: A downward movement can count as directional when it carries the moth away from a source above it. A dive can carry a moth away from an overhead speaker, so the path, not the dive, marks direction. Roeder's photographs made each insect's path visible for that judgment. Roeder applied that path-based definition throughout the trials.

Roeder enclosed the camera, which reduced the unwanted ultrasound produced by its shutter. The enclosure removed an artifact that the camera itself introduced. Stationary-flight preparations can restrict turning and may disturb the animal before a test. Roeder instead watched insects that entered the sound field during their own flights. Each trial was judged by the moth's path after onset.

Pooling different maneuvers into one rigid reflex would discard the variation recorded in free flight. Roeder's records keep turning, diving and climbing as separate responses to the same sound. Each response is a different motor solution to the acoustic threat. The records cover responses from weaker and stronger sources. Those responses were measured in natural flight.

inserts.title: Evasion was scored from the flight itself
paragraphs: Evasion was scored from the flight itself. A moth could be evasive and still be captured. Keeping movement and outcome apart prevents a circular definition of escape behavior. Surviving the encounter tells nothing about the maneuver itself. The authors recorded capture or escape for every encounter. The authors used infrared video to record each sequence.

Moth species, body form and flight performance also differed between the evasive and non-evasive groups. Those traits could also affect capture, alongside the maneuvers themselves. Successful evasion needs analysis of the maneuver itself, not just the sensory signal behind it. Flight performance was measured from the same reconstructed paths.

The study covered real pursuit and evasion in one outdoor enclosure. The moth assemblage in that enclosure limits how far the results extend to other habitats and predator species. A different set of moths would test that boundary. Each encounter was scored from the recorded path and its outcome. The results apply to this enclosure.
notes: Evasion was scored from the flight itself.

inserts.title: Sound-driven spikes mark peripheral input
paragraphs: The nerve had been separated from the central ganglion in the original preparation. Sound-evoked activity arose in the periphery, not from a feedback command sent by the brain. That separation kept central input out of the recording. The sensory side alone was sampled. The preparation kept the nerve's sensory output intact.

The non-acoustic discharge commonly occurred at 5 to 20 spikes per second. Separating that activity from sound-evoked spikes keeps every nerve event from counting as hearing. The regular firing of that unit gave a clear baseline for the sound-driven trains. Only two acoustic units followed the sound in these recordings.

Two acoustic units responded to sound, and the regular unit did not. Their thresholds separated the two responding units in the same nerve. The recorded thresholds identify the cells, not the spike forms. Roeder and Treat recorded both kinds of unit in the same preparation. Their thresholds were distinct even where spike sizes overlapped.

Suprathreshold responses and frequency-modulated bat calls were not tested in the same way, so the control leaves those responses untested. Validation applies to the measured range rather than to every stimulus the preparation could receive. The pure-tone conditions set the boundary of that validation.

The same moth served in every condition. Nerve electrodes went into the third condition alone. Each condition was set against the others within one animal. Individual differences stay out of the analysis. Velocity and displacement were both measured at each condition. The conditions for each moth were run in sequence.

paragraphs: Gordon and ter Hofstede compared the two cells across frequency using extracellular nerve recordings. Each cell adds its own threshold to the range of sound levels the nerve can signal. Gordon and ter Hofstede separated the cells by their threshold curves. A threshold gap is a property of the recording, not a behavior.

Frequency-dependent sensitivity can exist without an output that identifies sound frequency. That is a property of the nerve's response, not of a pitch judgment made by the moth. inserts.title: Latency shortens as sound grows stronger
paragraphs: Roeder measured tympanic responses to brief pulses presented in succession. He stepped the amplitude up in calibrated increments against each preparation's threshold. Responses near threshold were measured at 1 dB increments, which gave fine resolution at the lowest levels. Timing and spike count were measured at each step.

The external onset marker permits this latency measurement. Timing was more variable near threshold, which is when the stimulus is weakest. Some of that delay is axonal conduction from the receptor to the recording site. The delay is reported after that correction. The delay was measured in the same preparations at each level.

Roeder and Treat's section shows the attachment that drives this receptor, a structure in the ear rather than in the brain. A flying moth lacks an external marker and must obtain timing from its own sensory signals. Roeder's latency values came from a single preparation. The section is a published reconstruction, not a live recording.
notes: Latency shortens as sound grows stronger.

inserts.title: Summation and steering are separate questions
paragraphs: Roeder's matched pulses kept intensity constant across the three ear conditions. The recording coordinates place the units within the thoracic ganglia, where flight control circuits sit. Simultaneous stimulation of both ears was included. Each ear received the same stimulus pattern. The units sat near the midline of the ganglion.

The summating unit responded to both sides rather than to one. A unit's response to both ears leaves the stronger side unidentified. Steering needs side-specific information, and this unit lacks it. Roeder kept the summating response apart from the steering question. The unit's firing was measured in the same recordings.

The proposed steering mechanisms were not resolved by this summating response. Roeder distinguished this summation from the steering mechanism he had hypothesized, and the two ideas answer different questions about the same ganglion. Convergence of auditory inputs is one result, and a directional difference detector is a further one.
notes: Summation and steering are separate questions.

inserts.title: Duration sets the threshold of each cell

Pulse duration was the only variable in the tested set. Gordon and ter Hofstede reported threshold differences in decibels. A1 showed the steeper change of the two cells. A2 thresholds fell more gradually across the durations. A1 is the more sensitive of the two cells at every duration. Heliothis virescens is one of the species in which this pattern was measured. Those thresholds are reported in dB SPL.

Bat calls differ in two cues, duration and level, that the ear must combine. A comparison of bat calls must account for their duration as well as their level at the ear. Duration and level together set which calls a moth can detect. The duration effect is measured at the nerve, not at the moth's behavior. The same measurements covered two moth families.

inserts.title: Interval timing is a second intensity code
paragraphs: The experiment tested two claims about timing. One asked whether spikes form a burst. The other asked whether spacing inside the burst encodes extra intensity differences. The question was whether timing carries intensity information once spike count saturates. Gordon and ter Hofstede examined both claims in A1 recordings. The two claims were tested in the same recordings.

A reliable short interval can add to central excitation, even when it changes little across the plateau. Those intervals came from the short-pulse condition, where spike count saturated. Roeder's earlier recordings showed that tight bursts differ from isolated spikes. That range is where spike count stayed flat across levels. The plateau is the setting for these interval measures.

Pooled curves can look smoother than any single animal's response. One individual's plateau can occur at a different relative amplitude from another's. Spacing carries timing information that the spike count omits. Each moth's receptor output sets its own plateau. The meaningful event here is the burst itself. Burst spacing and spike count are separate readouts.
notes: Interval timing is a second intensity code.

inserts.title: Tiger-moth clicks respond to call timing
paragraphs: The clicking thresholds came from a laboratory playback of pulses with set intervals. Each interval represented a stage of bat echolocation. Playback intensity rose across the tested range. The thresholds came from the same playback design across intervals, with silent gaps between presentations. The first click is the measured endpoint of each playback.

This definition ties the threshold to the defensive output rather than to the sensory response alone. The threshold measures an action, not a receptor. Each click response was checked against the interval it followed. Clicks were scored as the moth's defensive output, not as its hearing. The sensory cells were never tested in isolation.

Rapid terminal timing required sound at higher levels than late approach timing did. Late approach calls at 20 to 30 ms triggered clicking at the lowest sound levels. The clicks themselves are the output that the threshold tracks. Hearing a pulse and emitting a defensive click are different measured events.

inserts.title: Bats raise intensity before a moth clicks
paragraphs: Corcoran and colleagues measured the bat's call levels over the 250 ms before clicking began. Those levels increased before the click. The claim concerns changes that come before a measured behavioral event. Both changes preceded the defensive output in the recorded encounters. Received level was measured at the moth in each encounter.

The bat's pulse intervals shortened slightly during the same interval. Shorter intervals and rising received intensity together marked the approach that preceded the moth's defense. The timing change was small next to the level change. Both measurements came from the same calls. Received level and interval are measured against the same clicking onset.

The authors proposed that selection favored efficient timing of the bat's calls. Field records alone leave that evolutionary history untested. The first click was the behavioral event used to time these changes. The proposal is a hypothesis about evolution, not a measured result. The proposal explains the timing pattern as a product of selection.

High radial acceleration allows rapid redirection, while the angle sets where that redirection places the moth relative to interception. Radial acceleration is a rate of change of direction. Both values came from one set of reconstructed paths. Successful maneuvers were set against failed ones on this measure. Larger angles marked the captured prey.

The sensory and motor mechanisms that choose the trajectory were not identified. The measured flight paths show which geometries worked. Trajectory choice was not measured directly in these encounters. Escape angle and radial acceleration remain the measured variables of this study. inserts.title: Tymbal removal raises bat contact rates
paragraphs: The same moth species was tested with and without the ability to click. That design helped separate sound production from differences among prey species. Each moth type was presented to the same bats. Silent palatable moths were the controls in these trials. The moths in the flight room were the same species used throughout.

Contact was the measured endpoint, which is distinct from consumption or long-term survival. Tethering restricts evasive flight, and organ removal is a physical manipulation. Ablation removed the tymbals from the clicking moths. Contact rates were recorded for each moth type. Each contact was recorded during the attack sequence. Tethered moths were the subjects in the same room.

The experiment shows that sound production matters in this preparation, not every ecological benefit of the species. The bats' contact rates changed with the tymbal, the one variable tested. Tymbal removal altered the contact outcome for the same bats. The intervention is stronger evidence than observing clicks near a missed capture alone.

2: Free-flying moths changed course or stopped beating their wings when artificial ultrasound reached them. Ultrasound is sound above the range humans can hear. Roeder photographed these moths on an open lawn, so each insect flew without a wire or tether. Each insect appeared as its own photographic track, which kept every flight path separate.

A **marker flash** showed exactly when the sound started. Breaks in the photographic tracks marked a 0.25-second time base, so each reaction could be timed from onset. Trials with the flash alone caused no change in the flight path. That timing control distinguishes the sound's effect from the visible flash.

Some moths made **passive dives** with motionless wings. Others kept flying under their own power. Reaction times ranged from 0.2 seconds to more than one second after the sound began. The sound produced several flight responses rather than one fixed reflex. Bright illumination and mixed species were features of these field observations.
3: At longer distances, or when the **ultrasonic output** fell, moths turned and flew away from the loudspeaker. The avoidance changed the direction of the flight path relative to the source, which mattered more than the change in height. Roeder recorded this response in moths that were free to fly. Direction referred to how the insect's path lay against the ultrasonic source.

The speaker stayed in one fixed position while naturally flying moths crossed an illuminated area. Moths that approached the source could reverse course. Insects below the source sometimes descended, and insects above it could turn upward. The lamp provided the light gradient that the moths crossed during each trial. Each moth's path was judged against that single fixed position.

Moths turned away whether the new path carried them toward, away from or across the light gradient. Light position alone did not decide the turn. The turns show that sound helped set the direction of flight. Those turns happened across all three path types, including paths that crossed the gradient.
4: Moths closer to the **transducer** performed a range of **escape maneuvers**. These included sharp passive dives, powered dives, loops, tight turns and climbs followed by descents. Most of these movements carried the moths toward the ground. The moths did not all head in one uniform direction away from the source. Each maneuver was judged from the photographed flight path.

Roeder usually repeated ultrasonic pulses 30 times per second. The sound continued while the flight was photographed. That design allowed observers to separate the path after sound onset from the movement the moth had already started. Each maneuver was recorded in free flight rather than on a restraining wire. The trajectory after onset could be read directly from the photographs.

Wing movements could stop or speed up after stimulation. A climb before a dive and continued wingbeats during a turn were different responses to one stimulus. The records show weaker sources producing avoidance and stronger sources producing diving. Stronger stimulation changed the form of the response, not only its direction.
5: Corcoran and Conner recorded long-legged myotis bats, _Myotis volans_, chasing naturally flying moths in an outdoor enclosure. **Infrared cameras** tracked predator and prey positions. The bats pursued moths that flew freely in the enclosure. This setup avoided the visible floodlighting that Roeder's photographic method required. The enclosure was outdoors, so the bats hunted under natural conditions.

Synchronized camera views were combined into **three-dimensional trajectories**. The enclosure measured 6 by 4 meters and stood 2.2 to 3 meters high. Calibration assigns a common spatial coordinate system to the camera recordings. Each reconstructed path was matched to the outcome of its encounter, whether the moth escaped or was captured. Released moths were allowed to fly naturally before attacks were analyzed.

A turn seen from one camera can hide changes in altitude or depth. Reconstructed paths measure those components directly. They also give speed and turning performance for each moth. The paths show how each moth moved in space relative to the bat. The measured paths are trajectories through a volume, not drawings inferred from one photograph.
6: In the observed encounters, bats captured 37.5 percent of **evasive prey** and 98 percent of **non-evasive prey**. A moth counted as evasive when it made sharp turns or accelerations during the attack. Survival in this setting depended heavily on that maneuver. An evasive moth could still be captured, so the outcome and the maneuver were recorded separately.

**Infrared video** matched each movement sequence to capture or escape. Non-evasive moths followed slow or broad paths. Evasive moths changed speed or direction abruptly as the bat approached. Each movement sequence was recorded from the approach through to the capture or escape. The timing of each abrupt change was logged against the bat's position.

The authors measured kinematics to explain why some evasive paths succeeded and others failed. Kinematics here means the speed, turning and acceleration of each path. These measurements compare the maneuvers that escaped with those that were caught. Survival alone says little about the maneuver, so the measured paths carry the explanation.
7: A **tympanum** is a thin membrane that vibrates in response to airborne sound. After moth clicks began, bats sometimes lengthened their pulse intervals and returned to an earlier attack stage before resuming pursuit. These reversals occurred in roughly one third of clicking-moth attacks and persisted with experience. The reversals continued as the bats gained experience with clicking prey. The reversals were recorded over repeated sessions.

Clicks disrupted the hunting sequence rather than ending it at the first click. Call timing marks the change in pursuit, but the bats' perceived distance to the moth was never measured. Clicks changed the sequence of calls that followed. The authors compared attack progression across silent and clicking moths. Attacks on silent moths showed the normal stage order.
45: Sound reception, neural coding and defensive behavior are separate experimental outcomes. Wax-moth recordings showed spikes to 300 kHz sound, and no flight test covered that frequency. Each outcome needs its own measurement. A nerve response alone says little about flight. The wax-moth recordings and the noctuid plateau come from different preparations.

In noctuid moths, a short-pulse A1 plateau codes intensity coarsely through spike count, despite a clear auditory response. A receptor can register the presence of sound without reporting every change in its amplitude. The wax-moth traces separate spikes that follow sound from spontaneous spikes. The short-pulse plateau is one example of that gap.

Turning those signals into behavior needs central recordings, interventions and measured escape or clicking responses. Roeder's pulse-marker observations and the later flight and tymbal experiments each address a different step in that chain. Together they trace the path from ear to defense one step at a time. Measured escape and clicking responses are the endpoints of that chain.
